L350@P12: LogisticsandTransportation
L351@P12: The BRP recommendations associated with
L352@P12: transportation underscore the importance of having
L353@P12: a range of logistics options available for supporting
L354@P12: research in the field.
L355@P12: NSF has worked to diversify these options through
L356@P12: extensive research and development of overland
L357@P12: traverse capabilities, and also by integrating new
L358@P12: fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft in support of the
L359@P12: USAP over the last fifteen years.
L360@P12: South Pole Traverse. NSF will incorporate
L361@P12: robotics technology, a project with a very high
L362@P12: return on investment, in the overland traverse
L363@P12: platform. This technology will reduce the cost of
L364@P12: resupplying South Pole Station while improving the
L365@P12: efficiency of the operation. The goal is to double
L366@P12: the number of traverses to South Pole from two to
L367@P12: four by FY 2016, achieving an estimated net annual
L368@P12: savings of $2.0 million dollars. To achieve this
L369@P12: aggressive goal, NSF is working with other Federal
L370@P12: agencies and industry to integrate commercial offthe-shelf products into the traverse fleet.

L386@P13: An ancillary benefit of further developing the
L387@P13: traverse platform is the opportunity it affords for
L388@P13: future research. As previously demonstrated, science
L389@P13: enabled by traverse can take many forms. For
L390@P13: example, paleoclimate studies were undertaken as
L391@P13: part of the traverse-supported International TransAntarctic Science Expedition (ITASE) before and
L392@P13: during the International Polar Year. The exploration
L393@P13: via clean drilling of a subglacial lake under the
L394@P13: Whillans Ice Stream during the 2012-2013 season
L395@P13: also capitalized on traverse support.
L396@P13: LC-130 Fleet Reduction and South Pole
L397@P13: Hard Surface Runway. NSF is engaged with its
L398@P13: Department of Defense (DoD) partners to explore the
L399@P13: feasibility of implementing other recommendations
L400@P13: made by the Panel. Two primary topics under
L401@P13: discussion are the recommendations to reduce the
L402@P13: operational LC-130 fleet from ten to six aircraft, and
L403@P13: to construct a compacted snow runway at South Pole
L404@P13: Station to allow wheeled aircraft operations. While
L405@P13: NSF believes that construction of such a runway
L406@P13: is technically feasible, there are many operational
L407@P13: issues associated with landing wheeled aircraft at
L408@P13: the South Pole (such as infrastructure and equipment
L409@P13: for fire and emergency response, refueling, and
L410@P13: cargo handling) that must be understood in order to
L411@P13: conduct a cost-benefit analysis. Such an analysis
L412@P13: would also need to take into account cost savings
L413@P13: and efficiencies gained as a result of reducing the
L414@P13: population at South Pole Station and increasing the
L415@P13: traverse capabilities. A further complicating factor for
L416@P13: USAP air support is the seasonal warming that has
L417@P13: been impacting wheeled operations at McMurdo’s
L418@P13: Pegasus Runway. For the past three seasons, local
L419@P13: temperature conditions have limited wheeled aircraft
L420@P13: operations during the mid-December to late-January
L421@P13: timeframe. In December 2012, the runway became
L422@P13: completely unusable for wheeled aircraft due to
L423@P13: melting exacerbated by volcanic dust blown from
L424@P13: Black Island; portions of the snow road from Pegasus
L425@P13: to McMurdo were also made impassable to all but
L426@P13: tracked vehicles. During this period of time, only
L427@P13: LC-130 aircraft enabled access between New Zealand
L428@P13: and locations within Antarctica. These recent
L429@P13: developments are causing NSF to review whether
L430@P13: further consolidation at the Pegasus site and increased
L431@P13: reliance on wheeled aircraft are advisable.
L432@P13: McMurdo and Palmer Faci lities
L433@P13: The BRP recommended that aging facilities be
L434@P13: upgraded according to master plans in order to
L435@P13: reduce operating costs and increase efficiency for
L436@P13: science support.
L437@P13: NSF is currently in the process of updating the
L438@P13: master plans for both McMurdo and Palmer
L439@P13: Stations. For McMurdo, the Master Plan is in the
L440@P13: final stages of development. The Master Plan
L441@P13: addresses most of the large-scale investments
L442@P13: recommended by the Panel for operational efficiency
L443@P13: and safety. For example, it seeks to minimize the
L444@P13: need to handle materials multiple times, to improve
L445@P13: energy efficiency and to consolidate functions to
L446@P13: reduce personnel requirements. Activities are being
L447@P13: sequenced in discrete phases to ensure continuity of
L448@P13: operations as upgrades proceed. A Palmer Station
L449@P13: Systems Study was released in 2010. This study
L450@P13: considered some of the health and usability issues
L451@P13: that were raised by the BRP. In accordance with the
L452@P13: BRP’s recommendation, an in-depth study of the fire
L453@P13: suppression systems at all USAP operating locations
L454@P13: will be undertaken in FY 2014. In the near-term,
L455@P13: NSF has continued to take steps to ensure that fire
L456@P13: protection systems are fully operational in critical
L457@P13: facilities in Antarctica such as berthing and food
L458@P13: preparation areas. NSF will consider the results of
L459@P13: these studies and update its long-range investment
L460@P13: plan, discussed below, for priority investments.
L461@P13: The USAP recently upgraded the emergency response
L462@P13: equipment at McMurdo Station. Credit: George Blaisdell,
L463@P13-14: National Science Foundation5
L464@P14: Specific to boating operations at Palmer Station,
L465@P14: NSF has taken actions to improve the safety and
L466@P14: efficiency of boating operations at Palmer Station.
L467@P14: NSF is working on assessments in preparation
L468@P14: for replacing the pier and mitigating a hazardous
L469@P14: underwater rock ledge that currently limits the
L470@P14: size of vessels that can directly access the station.
L471@P14: An improved pier is expected to take two years
L472@P14: to complete once funding has been identified. In
L473@P14: the meantime, a temporary fender system is being
L474@P14: employed to keep docked ships away from the
L475@P14: underwater obstruction. Safety concerns related
L476@P14: to small boat embarkation/disembarkation have
L477@P14: been resolved through installation of a floating
L478@P14: dock at Palmer Station. The Antarctic Support
L479@P14: Contractor is working with vendors to finalize
L480@P14: requirements for RIBs (rigid-hull inflatable boats)
L481@P14: that are expected to be delivered and operational
L482@P14: in FY 2014 to safely extend science operations
L483@P14: farther from the station than is currently possible.
L484@P14: A boat ramp to facilitate safe launch and recovery
L485@P14: of all small craft has been designed and is
L486@P14: scheduled to be constructed and operational in
L487@P14: this same timeframe.
L488@P14: USAP Capital Budget
L489@P14: In order to improve and maintain USAP facilities
L490@P14: and infrastructure, the BRP recommended that NSF
L491@P14: establish a capital plan and budget for the Program.
L492@P14: NSF agrees that planning tools are needed to guide
L493@P14: its longer-term approach to improvements and
L494@P14: maintenance within the constraints of the federal
L495@P14: budgeting process.
L496@P14: NSF has developed a Long-Range Investment
L497@P14: Plan (LRIP) and associated budget, using
L498@P14: myriad inputs including needs identified by
L499@P14: the user communities consisting of support
L500@P14: contract employees, DoD partners, NSF-funded
L501@P14: researchers, and other agencies relying on USAP
L502@P14: support in Antarctica. The LRIP is also informed
L503@P14: by other long-range planning activities in which
L504@P14: NSF regularly engages, such as the updates for
L505@P14: Palmer and McMurdo Stations that are currently
L506@P14: underway. These updates entail a complete
L507@P14: review of current requirements, an assessment
L508@P14: of current facilities and equipment to meet
L509@P14: requirements, and recommendations for corrective
L510@P14: action and improvements.
L511@P14: As needs are identified, project proposals will be
L512@P14: generated and prioritized against factors such as
L513@P14: mission criticality, alignment to vision, program
L514@P14: interface, cost/benefit, risk assessment, and
L515@P14: readiness (among others). A project will be added
L516@P14: to the LRIP in accord with the determination of its
L517@P14: priority. NSF will adopt a portfolio management
L518@P14: approach to lifecycle management, which will be
L519@P14: built into the LRIP over time to sequence major
L520@P14: investments such as vehicle fleet replacement and
L521@P14: major maintenance. The LRIP captures planned
L522@P14: and in-process capital investments in terms of
L523@P14: budget outlays and cash inflows. Budget Outlays
L524@P14: are categorized according to Capital Investments
L525@P14: and Life Cycle Support. Cash Inflows become
L526@P14: available as projects are completed, through
L527@P14: appropriations, and from returns on investments
L528@P14: already made. The LRIP is constructed to provide
L529@P14: a high-level view of outlays and inflows over a
L530@P14: rolling five-year period.
L531@P14: The LRIP process represents a further step in
L532@P14: improving the USAP’s budget structure, but for
L533@P14: this system to be effective, significant management
L534@P14: attention—and discipline—will need to be paid to
L535@P14: avoid encroachment on these funds by competing
L536@P14: priorities within the overall infrastructure and
L537@P14: logistics budget. Stakeholders within Polar
L538@P14: Programs have agreed that the LRIP budget is
L539@P14: appropriately and adequately sized and have
L540@P14: pledged to respect the designation of these funds
L541@P14: for investments.

L544@P14: boating operations in support of marine research. Credit:

L550@P15: Science Support Costs
L551@P15: The BRP recommended that NSF further
L552@P15: strengthen the process by which the fully burdened
L553@P15: cost and technological readiness of research
L554@P15: instrumentation and observing systems, as well as
L555@P15: overall projects, are considered in the review and
L556@P15: selection of science projects.
L557@P15: NSF agrees that increased cost awareness could
L558@P15: be beneficial. This recommendation reinforces
L559@P15: NSF actions over the last several years to bring
L560@P15: greater cost awareness to proposal reviewers via
L561@P15: discussions of operational support, and to principal
L562@P15: investigators during the award negotiation process.
L563@P15: The actions are evolving as NSF and the Antarctic
L564@P15: Support Contractor improve the robustness of cost
L565@P15: information. NSF engaged the services of the expert
L566@P15: who supported the BRP to complete development of
L567@P15: the cost model that will identify discrete elements
L568@P15: of cost and make it easier to predict the impacts
L569@P15: on cost of various actions. Once completed, the
L570@P15: cost model will be a useful tool for developing
L571@P15: messaging related to costs for the USAP community.
L572@P15: This cost model, along with continual improvement
L573@P15: of science project planning activities, will also be
L574@P15: useful for developing budget plans for the evolving
L575@P15: science program and for ensuring that NSF can
L576@P15: protect commitments that are made. It will aid in
L577@P15: understanding the impacts of funding fluctuations in
L578@P15: the USAP budget as well. In short, it will assist NSF
L579@P15: in making well-informed and balanced decisions
L580@P15: about USAP operations.
L581@P15: NSF will expand pre-deployment testing and
L582@P15: evaluation activities now used for larger and more
L583@P15: complex projects. For example, both the deep
L584@P15: ice core drill and the CReSIS (Center for Remote
L585@P15: Sensing of Ice Sheets) radar technologies were
L586@P15: tested extensively in Greenland before being
L587@P15: deployed in Antarctica. NSF has also strengthened

L599@P15: and retrieval of scientific instrumentation.

L603@P15: as defining milestones for development and testing,
L604@P15: establishing criteria for evaluating whether or
L605@P15: not milestones are met, and conducting readiness
L606@P15: reviews prior to deployment. These changes

L648@P16: Communications
L649@P16: The BRP recommended that NSF modernize
L650@P16: communication capabilities in Antarctica and the
L651@P16: Southern Ocean to enable increased science output
L652@P16: and reduce operational footprint.
L653@P16: NSF appreciates the value of communications for
L654@P16: science and operations and works to balance needs
L655@P16: and desires through evaluation of requirements,
L656@P16: cost/benefit analyses, and implementation of
L657@P16: alternatives. NSF currently has the capability to
L658@P16: provide high-bandwidth communications to all
L659@P16: Antarctic field sites, although not continuously at all
L660@P16: sites. Data-intensive activities such as the IceCube
L661@P16: Neutrino Observatory and the South Pole Telescope
L662@P16: employ filtering and compression techniques
L663@P16: developed in partnership with other parts of NSF in
L664@P16: order to ensure that critical data are provided on a
L665@P16: near real-time basis. In addition, NSF maintains a
L666@P16: program for actively pursuing all available options
L667@P16: for improving high-bandwidth communications.
L668@P16: This program includes participation by other
L669@P16: agencies such as NASA and DoD. In preparation
L670@P16: for the BRP review, NSF funded an “analysis of
L671@P16: alternatives” for Antarctic communications that
L672@P16: reviewed requirements as well as the cost and
L673@P16: feasibility of a range of communications solutions.
L674@P16: There appear to be cost-effective solutions that
L675@P16: make use of satellites retired from other uses to meet
L676@P16: NSF needs for the foreseeable future.
L677@P16: Energy Efficiency
L678@P16: The BRP recommended that NSF increase energy
L679@P16: efficiency and implement renewable energy
L680@P16: technologies to reduce operational costs.
L681@P16: NSF agrees that maximizing the use of alternative
L682@P16: and renewable energies at all operating locations
L683@P16: is a necessary goal given the rising cost of fuel.
L684@P16: Significant strides have been made in this area, driving
L685@P16: down annual fuel consumption through reductions
L686@P16: in personnel and the overall operational tempo. For
L687@P16: example, during the 2012-13 season, the population
L688@P16: at South Pole Station was reduced from 250 to 168
L689@P16: personnel, resulting in a 30% reduction in fuel usage at
L690@P16: the station. Additional study to determine the optimal
L691@P16: use of these resources will be needed. The study will
L692@P16: necessarily draw on the long-range planning activity
L693@P16: that is currently underway for McMurdo and the
L694@P16: Palmer Station Systems Study. Projects to implement
L695@P16: improvements will be included in the LRIP.
L696@P16: In the short-term, NSF and Antarctica New
L697@P16: Zealand (AntNZ) continue to work cooperatively

L723@P17: International Cooperation
L724@P17: The BRP recommended that NSF pursue additional
L725@P17: opportunities for international cooperation in shared
L726@P17: logistics support as well as scientific endeavors.
L727@P17: As previously noted, NSF is actively pursuing
L728@P17: additional opportunities to leverage resources with
L729@P17: our international partners. For example, pursuant
L730@P17: to more general agreements to cooperate, annual
L731@P17: implementation plans that benefit the USAP are
L732@P17: developed with international partners. Such
L733@P17: arrangements are discussed year-round through
L734@P17: recurring face-to-face meetings, frequent e-mail and
L735@P17: telephone contact, and through the annual meetings
L736@P17: of COMNAP and SCAR (Scientific Committee
L737@P17: on Antarctic Research, an advisory body to the
L738@P17: Antarctic Treaty). NSF engages with other national
L739@P17: programs through international organizations such
L740@P17: as COMNAP to look for opportunities to standardize
L741@P17: equipment and take advantage of volume pricing.
L742@P17: NSF is also looking to expand arrangements in
L743@P17: the Ross Sea region as well as in the Antarctic
L744@P17: Peninsula. Countries including Australia, Italy,
L745@P17: France, South Korea, and New Zealand have active
L746@P17: logistics programs and bases in the Ross Sea region
L747@P17: and represent cost-sharing opportunities for the
L748@P17: USAP, while several countries offer opportunities
L749@P17: in the Peninsula area. NSF will continue to work
L750@P17: with our international partners to ensure active and
L751@P17: open data sharing that is a hallmark of the Antarctic
L752@P17: Treaty and facilitates more efficient science. NSF partners with the Department of Energy to identify
L753@P17: opportunities to expand the USAP’s use of alternative and
L754@P17: renewable energy, such as the electric vehicles that are now in use
L755@P17: at McMurdo Station. Credit: Peter Rejcek, Antarctic Support Contract
